A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PC Agent-E research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, mathematical notation, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original agent evaluations on WindowsAgentArena-V2 and OSWorld, training-data and test-time scaling experiments, and qualitative failure analysis.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds distillation comparisons, a smaller-model experiment, original-WindowsAgentArena scores, and extended test-time evaluation.

M1.justification: The proposed pipeline remains human trajectory collection, Claude thought completion, nine alternative decisions per human state, and supervised training with the same ReAct scaffold. The prompts are substantively unchanged. The additional 7B experiment applies the existing method, while direct distillation is a comparison method.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the 312 Windows training tasks and Windows/Linux evaluation coverage. v2 newly reports original-WindowsAgentArena scores, but v1 already explicitly describes evaluating that benchmark in Section 4. The smaller-model and longer-step experiments change configurations rather than represented tasks or domains.

E2.justification: v2 adds GPT-4o to the main benchmark comparison, direct distillation and human-plus-distillation training baselines, NAVI to the original-WindowsAgentArena comparison, and Qwen2.5-VL-7B as the smaller-model reference. The distillation controls substantially expand comparison of the proposed training strategy against alternatives.

E3.justification: New protocols include collecting ten end-to-end Claude trajectories per training task, a control combining one human trajectory with nine Claude trajectories per task, training a 7B backbone, and evaluating a 50-step limit. Existing 72B training settings and the main 30-step evaluation remain unchanged. The newly specified decontamination thresholds document an existing procedure.

E4.justification: Section 5.4 and Appendices C–E add tests of whether direct distillation or mixed human/teacher data can replace Trajectory Boost, whether the method benefits a smaller model, and whether scaling remains effective beyond 30 steps. The 50-step experiment adds a substantive termination-failure analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-evaluation counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. The ten Claude trajectories per task in v2 describe training-data collection, not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Shared benchmark scores and existing scaling points are unchanged. New results include direct and mixed distillation scores of 26.2% and 26.9% versus PC Agent-E's 36.0%, original-WindowsAgentArena scores of 27.9% versus NAVI's 19.5%, and 7B scores of 6.4% versus 5.0%. At 50 steps, PC Agent-E scores 31.4%, below its retained 30-step score of 36.0%. v2 also reports synthesis times of approximately 3 versus 900 hours.

T1.justification: The environment-snapshot and trajectory-history formalization is unchanged. Replacing v1's scaling-factor notation s′ with v2's s preserves the same augmented-action ratio. Neither version contains substantive theoretical results or proofs that are added, removed, or revised.

C1.justification: v2 makes greater effectiveness and efficiency than direct distillation a central claim in the abstract, contribution list, and conclusion. It also shifts the headline comparison from outperforming thinking-enabled Claude to outperforming the non-thinking teacher by approximately 10%, while describing thinking-Claude performance as comparable. The 141% improvement over the base model remains.

C2.justification: v2 explains the distillation gap through avoidance of accumulated rollout errors, attributes limited 7B gains to knowledge and grounding deficiencies, and qualifies test-time scaling through termination failures beyond the training horizon. These substantially expand mechanism and applicability discussions. v1's separate resource-limitations section and discussion of complementary RL/SFT development are removed.

D1.justification: v2 specifies previously vague decontamination cutoffs: zero 13-gram overlap, 3-gram overlap below 0.7, and cosine similarity below 0.85. It also reports synthesis runtimes, but omits v1's explicit random-subsampling description for smaller augmentation factors. Training hyperparameters, prompt content, tracker instructions, and the resource link are retained.

R1.justification: The native-agent and data-synthesis taxonomy remains largely intact. v2 adds GPT-4 and OmniParser references for the NAVI comparison, removes several earlier trajectory-collection, agent-framework, and reasoning/RL citations, and more explicitly distinguishes Trajectory Boost from direct distillation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution statements, experimental narrative, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around the teacher-distillation comparison. Experiments are organized around explicit research questions, the standalone limitations section disappears, and the appendix structure expands while retaining the relocated prompts and tracker manual. An LLM writing-assistance disclosure is added.

P2.justification: v2 removes the example-trajectory figure, separates v1's two-panel scaling figure into individual figures, and adds a direct-distillation curve. It adds a trajectory-length table and four appendix result tables, expands the main comparison table, and reformats the document in the ICLR style. Most pipeline illustrations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct-distillation controls; v2 adds both direct and human-plus-distillation comparisons, materially strengthening evidence for the specific value of Trajectory Boost. The 7B experiment and the performance decline at 50 steps also establish useful limits to the method's applicability and scaling claims. Removing the earlier limitations discussion weakens transparency, and uncertainty reporting remains absent, but the new controls and better-qualified conclusions provide a substantial overall improvement.
